newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Storm clouds gather on Brazil civil service reform.
newsitem.headline: Storm clouds gather on Brazil civil service reform.

text.p: The chances of Brazil's civil service reform bill being put to a first vote in the Chamber of Deputies as scheduled on Wednesday looked slim as the government struggled to overcome opposition within allied parties.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso met with political leaders Tuesday to discuss obstacles in the reform's way.

"If we can, we'll vote on it tomorrow," said Political Coordination Minister Luiz Carlos Santos after the meeting. "It's not a matter of difficulties. We're talking and those talks haven't finished yet."
The civil service reform aims to reduce the burden of salaries and pensions for state and muncipal governments, many of which spend over 80 percent of receipts on payrolls.
Along with a pension reform bill, currently in the Senate, it represents one of the government's most powerful tools in curbing public spending.
But key clauses have already been watered down in an attempt to secure the two three-fifths majorities which the reform, as a constitutional amendment, requires in each chamber of Congress.
For example, the government originally wanted to give states and municipalities complete freedom to cut staff.

Instead, civil servants who enjoy job stability may only be dismissed in administrations that spend more than 60 percent of receipts on personnel costs, and only after cuts have been made to staff from other, less protected categories.
Now, 19 months after the reform was sent to Congress, a proposed 10,800 real ($10,285) ceiling on monthly pay and pensions included in it has met resistance in Congress.
Many lawmakers earn pensions from previous jobs in state and municipal administrations on top of their 8,000 real monthly salaries and stand to lose under the proposal.
Newspapers say 141 members of the Chamber of Deputies are in that situation, making it hard for the government to secure the three-fifths majority needed.

Another clause, allowing states and muncipalities to set the own "sub-ceilings" beneath the 10,800 real maximum is opposed by senior members of the judiciary. They say politicians would use the issue of pay to exert influence over judges.

Deputy Wellington Moreira Franco, who drew up the reform, said public opinion would be outraged if lawmakers and judges were exempted from the pay caps and insisted the vote would take place Wednesday.
But Congress-watchers say the reform has little chance of approval as it stands.
"I think discussion of the bill might start (Wednesday), but I don't think (the government) will manage to finish the subject off," said Carlos Lopes of consultants Santa Fe Ideias.

He said the government would probably only manage to hold the first of the two votes on the reform in early April. Lawmakers will stay away from Brasilia next week to take advantage of the Easter holiday.
